bull_thesis:
EFG International is a Zurich-based private bank -- it looks after the money of wealthy families across Switzerland, Europe, Asia and Latin America and is paid a fee on the assets it holds. The bull case is that this is a genuinely good franchise that just got marked down for the wrong reason.

Start with what is hard to fake. Client money has flowed in for fifteen consecutive half-years. In the first half of 2026 net new assets were CHF 5.7 billion, an annualised 6.2%, above the company's own 4-6% target range, and that follows CHF 11.3 billion (6.8%) in 2025. Assets under management crossed CHF 200 billion for the first time on 21 July 2026 when the Quilvest acquisition closed, up 23% in a year. Net profit for the half was CHF 185 million, the best six months in the company's history, and return on tangible equity -- profit measured against shareholders' capital excluding goodwill -- reached 22.4%, up three percentage points and already above the 20% goal set for 2028. Three of the four targets for the 2026-2028 cycle were met in the very first semester of that cycle.

Then look at where the growth is coming from. Net commission income, the recurring fee stream that is the actual moat, rose 20% to CHF 434 million while the commission margin held steady at 46 basis points (a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point). The part of the revenue that fell is the interest line -- down 12% to CHF 135 million as rates came down. That is a cycle, not a franchise problem, and it is exactly the distinction the market failed to make on 22 and 23 July, when the shares fell about 11.5% over three sessions on a profit that missed consensus by roughly 2%.

The balance sheet supports the case rather than threatening it. Common equity tier 1 capital -- the regulator's core solvency measure -- rose 100 basis points to 15.0% against a 12% internal floor, total capital is 18.3%, and the company generated 2.3% of capital organically in the half. The dividend has risen five years running; the CHF 0.65 for 2025 was paid on 30 March 2026. Management has also earned some benefit of the doubt: in November 2025 it told the market the revenue margin would land 'somewhere in the middle' between 95 and 85 basis points, and it landed at 90-91.

Finally, the profit engine has room to improve that is already contracted for. The cost-to-income ratio is 71.5% against a 68% target, and the gap exists because the acquired banks -- Cite Gestion, the New Zealand business and now Quilvest -- have not yet been migrated onto EFG's technology platform. That migration is scheduled for 2027. If it lands, the same revenue produces materially more profit, which is how management gets from the 5% growth it delivered this half to the roughly 15% a year it has promised for the cycle.

Conditions this case depends on: the commission margin holds at or near 46 basis points; net new money stays inside or above the 4-6% range; the 2027 platform migration delivers the cost synergies on schedule; world equity markets do not fall materially, since fee income moves with the value of client assets; and no new legacy legal provision of consequence lands.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that EFG is a bad business. It is that the reported earnings are lower quality than the headline suggests, that the price already reflects a good outcome, and that the one number that would prove the franchise is intact is the one management would not answer.

Take the earnings apart. Operating income in the first half of 2026 was CHF 856.5 million. Of that, CHF 434 million is durable fee income. CHF 135 million is net interest income and it is shrinking 12% a year. The remaining CHF 287 million is treasury swaps, trading and life insurance -- and management has told you both are impaired. On life insurance, in July 2026: 'we do expect it to wind down to zero as we move along in the next couple of years.' On the swap income, in February 2026, the chief financial officer explained that swap revenue rose on volume while 'the NII element decreased because it's the other side of the same equation' -- in plain words, part of the reported growth is interest income relabelled, not new economics. Strip both out over a few years and the profit base is smaller than CHF 370 million annualised.

Now the price EFG can charge. The revenue margin -- the yield the bank earns on every franc of client money -- fell to 91 basis points in the first half of 2026 from 97 a year earlier on management's own comparison, and from 104 on the reported basis that includes life insurance. Management frames this as successful defence toward an 85 basis point floor. It is still a falling price. And when Nicholas Herman asked the precise question -- why, in the footnotes, has the margin on advisory and management fees fallen sequentially -- the answer was a methodological objection ('you cannot just strip out one line and do the calculation'), not a number. The chief executive then partly conceded it: 'the volume effect was more important than the margin effect.' Assets grew; the price per franc of assets did not. Mandate penetration, the share of client assets under a paid advisory or discretionary mandate, has been stuck at 67% against a 75% goal, and the plan to fix it came with the disclaimer 'there is no guarantee on the outcomes.'

Costs went the wrong way. Cost-to-income was 69.8% for 2025 and 71.5% in the first half of 2026, leaving the one missed target 350 basis points away, with the fix -- the 2027 technology migration -- entirely in the future. Every cost synergy underwriting the 68% goal sits beyond the next reporting event, which is not until roughly February 2027.

The legal tail is a recurring cost, not a one-off. A CHF 45 million insurance recovery in the first half of 2025, a CHF 59 million provision in the second half; the trailing twelve months carry roughly CHF 107 million of one-off loss, which is why the trailing net margin reads 16.3% against 23.3% a year earlier. When Citi's Hannah Leivdal asked in February 2026 what gives management confidence there will be no further provisions, the answer was about capital adequacy, not about the cases.

Capital generation is partly a bookkeeping effect. Of the 2.3% organic build in the half, roughly 50 basis points is a non-cash add-back of share-based pay (CHF 80-90 million a year), and management confirmed the risk-weighted-asset optimisation that helped is largely finished: 'the biggest part of it has already been concluded in the first half of 2026.'

And there is nowhere for a corporate remedy to come from. Roughly 45% of the shares sit with EFG Bank European Financial Group, the Latsis family vehicle, and another 13-17% with BTG Pactual, which has been reducing a stake that was 30% when it sold BSI to EFG in 2016. With about 60% of the register closed and daily volume near 250,000 shares, there is no takeover premium available, no activist path, and a standing overhang if BTG sells more.

What would confirm the bear case: the commission margin slipping below 46 basis points at the full-year 2026 results; net new money dropping back inside or below the 4-6% range; cost-to-income staying above 71% after the 2027 migration; or a fresh legacy provision. Any of those, and a business earning roughly CHF 1.10 to CHF 1.15 a share on a de-rated multiple is worth something closer to CHF 12 than CHF 17.
consensus_delta:
The honest answer is that the market and this committee are not far apart -- and saying so is more useful than manufacturing a disagreement. Published analyst opinion sits at hold with a target cut to roughly CHF 18.40 after the results, against a base sum-of-the-parts value here of about CHF 17.25. That is a narrow gap. Where we do disagree, we disagree in two directions that largely cancel, which is exactly why there is no large mispricing to harvest.

First, the street is over-reading the revenue margin as a franchise problem. The headline yield on client assets fell to 91 basis points from 97 a year earlier, and Vontobel's note on the 22 July print attributed the roughly 2% profit miss to 'slightly weaker revenues than expected.' But the decline sits in the interest line, which fell 12% to CHF 135 million because rates fell. The fee margin -- the part that is actually the moat -- held at 46 basis points while fee income grew 20% to CHF 434 million. An 11.5% three-day de-rating on a 2% miss, while Julius Baer trades near its own 52-week high, is a market pricing the wrong line item.

Second, and pulling the other way, the street is giving too much credit to the words 'record profit.' A meaningful slice of that record is not durable. Life insurance is guided by management to 'wind down to zero as we move along in the next couple of years' (July 2026). Treasury swap income rose on volume while, in the chief financial officer's own February 2026 words, 'the NII element decreased because it's the other side of the same equation' -- part of the growth is interest income relabelled. And the capital build flatters too: of 2.3% organic generation in the half, roughly 50 basis points is a non-cash share-based-pay add-back, and management confirmed the risk-weighted-asset optimisation behind it 'has already been concluded in the first half of 2026.' Anyone capitalising CHF 370 million of annualised profit at a full multiple is capitalising something that is not all there.

There is a third disagreement, and it is with our own screening layer rather than with the street. The scan presents EFG with net cash of CHF 2.56 billion, free cash flow of minus CHF 2.43 billion, a return on invested capital of 1.8% and a solvency score of 0.4. Every one of those is an artifact of applying industrial-company tools to a bank. Taken literally, the first would invent roughly CHF 8.50 a share of value -- more than half the company -- and the last two would price it as a distressed, cash-burning business. The correct read is neither: common equity tier 1 capital is 15.0%, return on tangible equity is 22.4%, and the company generates capital organically every half.
forcing_function:
There is no hard date. That is the plain answer, and under this book's rules it is a descriptive fact rather than a mark against the name.

The two events capable of forcing a re-rating have already happened, in the same week: the Quilvest acquisition closed on 21 July 2026 and the first-half results were published on 22 July 2026. The next scheduled corporate events are the full-year 2026 results in roughly February 2027, followed by the dividend proposal, the annual general meeting and payment in roughly March 2027, on the pattern of the 20 March 2026 meeting and 30 March 2026 payment.

The genuine re-rating triggers are all undated, and each is testable at that February 2027 print:
1. The cost-to-income ratio breaking below 70% as the acquired banks migrate onto EFG's technology platform. This is the one target of four being missed, by 350 basis points, and the migration is guided for 2027. It is also the mechanism that converts the 5% profit growth delivered this half into the roughly 15% a year management has promised.
2. The commission margin holding at 46 basis points for a second consecutive half, with the total revenue margin stabilising at or above 90. This is the number that settles whether the July de-rating was about a rate cycle or about pricing power, and it is the exact question management declined to answer when Nicholas Herman put it to them in July 2026.
3. A resolution, or a final provision, on the remaining legacy legal cases -- the event that would empty an exceptional line that has not been empty in any recent period and let the market capitalise clean earnings.
4. A further BTG Pactual sell-down that clears the overhang and widens the free float. This would hurt on the day and help thereafter.
Absent those, the re-rating mechanism is simply compounding: about 6% annual organic asset growth at a 22.4% return on tangible equity, with capital building at roughly 2% a half.
valley_of_death:
For a deep-value candidate the question is whether something breaks before the discount closes. Nothing here threatens solvency; what threatens the thesis is a seven-month vacuum plus three live headwinds.

The information vacuum comes first. EFG reports twice a year. Having printed on 22 July 2026, the next scheduled disclosure is the full-year 2026 results in roughly February 2027. For the next seven months the shares drift on rate expectations, the dollar and the level of world equity markets, with no company-specific news to correct the de-rating. There is no buyback authorisation, no strategic review and no dividend event in that window.

Second, the fee base is directly geared to markets. Fee income is charged on client assets, so an equity drawdown cuts revenue roughly one-for-one with the fall in asset values, and the current regime read flags exactly that risk: positioning is full (the July fund-manager survey put cash at 3.6%, a formal sell signal), the equal-weight index has led all year, and volatility at about 18.5 is conspicuously cheap against a live oil shock, with Brent near $89 after the Hormuz blockade was reinstated on 14 July. A 10-15% market drawdown would take roughly the same off the revenue base and compress the multiple at the same time. This is the most underappreciated risk in the name: EFG looks like a compounder and behaves like leveraged exposure to the tape.

Third, rates. Under the current Federal Reserve leadership the priced base case is a hike by December, not a cut, and this thesis explicitly does not need a cut -- which is a point in its favour under the current regime, where rate-rescue theses are penalised. Higher dollar rates would actually help the interest line that has been shrinking. The offsetting risk is that the same higher rates weigh on asset prices and therefore on the fee base, and that a weak dollar keeps translating a 47% dollar-denominated asset book into fewer francs.

Fourth, the legal tail is the single most likely negative surprise. The exceptional line has not been empty in any recent period -- a CHF 45 million insurance recovery in the first half of 2025, a CHF 59 million provision in the second -- and the trailing twelve months carry roughly CHF 107 million of one-off loss. When asked in February 2026 what gives confidence that no further provisions are coming, management answered with capital adequacy rather than with the cases themselves.

Fifth, execution. Every cost synergy underwriting the 68% cost-to-income target depends on migrating the acquired banks onto EFG's platform in 2027. A slip pushes the target beyond the cycle and turns the 15%-a-year profit growth promise into the 5% actually delivered this half. There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall -- capital is 15.0% common equity tier 1 and 18.3% total -- so this is an earnings-quality and market-beta risk window, not a solvency one.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling mechanic available here, and that is itself the finding.

The register is closed. EFG Bank European Financial Group, the Latsis family vehicle, holds roughly 45%, and BTG Pactual retains roughly 13-17%, down from the 30% it received when it sold BSI to EFG in 2016. That leaves a free float around 40% on a company trading roughly 250,000 shares a day. Three consequences follow. Any further BTG sell-down is a standing overhang that would take many days of normal volume to absorb -- a slow bleed rather than a clean flush. There is no takeover-premium path, because control is not for sale. And there is no activist path either, which is why the classic special-situations screen fails this name on every leg: catalyst density is low, the sum-of-the-parts discount is small, and a governance reset or strategic process is structurally blocked by the control block. Do not underwrite this expecting someone to force the issue.

Nor is there a yield-holder liquidation to harvest. The dividend has risen five consecutive years, the CHF 0.65 for 2025 was paid on 30 March 2026, and nothing about the capital position (15.0% common equity tier 1, 2.3% organic generation in the half) suggests a cut. Income holders have no reason to leave.

What did happen on 22-24 July was a genuine but modest flush: 454,000 shares traded on results day, 775,000 the next session and 298,000 the day after, against a baseline near 250,000, taking the price from CHF 18.08 to CHF 15.98. That is roughly three days of elevated turnover -- real selling, but nowhere near capitulation. The shares now sit 7% up their 52-week range and about 22% below the 52-week high, while Julius Baer trades within 7% of its own high. The absence of a sector move is what makes this interesting; the absence of a capitulation is what argues for patience. If the market drawdown the regime read warns about arrives, the deeper flush -- and the better entry -- comes with it.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a good business at a fair price, marked down for a reason that is only half right -- and that is not the same thing as an opportunity.

What is genuinely strong: fifteen consecutive half-years of client inflows, running at 6.2% annualised against a 4-6% target; a return on tangible equity that rose three percentage points to 22.4% and cleared the 2028 goal in the first semester of the cycle; fee income up 20% with the fee margin steady at 46 basis points; capital at 15.0% common equity tier 1 against a 12% internal floor; and a management team that has hit the multi-year targets it set for itself and even called its own margin landing point correctly nine months in advance. Three of four cycle targets were met at the cycle's start.

What holds it back: the earnings are lower quality than the headline. Of CHF 856.5 million of first-half operating income, roughly a third is treasury swap carry, trading and a life-insurance contribution that management has guided to zero within about two years -- and the chief financial officer has said in plain terms that the swap income is the other side of the shrinking interest line, not new economics. Costs went the wrong way, to 71.5% against a 68% target, with the fix entirely in 2027. The exceptional line is never empty. And roughly 60% of the register is closed, so there is no takeover premium, no activist and no corporate remedy -- only compounding.

Priced properly, that lands close to today's quote. The parts sum to about CHF 17.25 a share against CHF 16.10 -- roughly 7% -- and the cross-checks (13 times 2027 consensus at CHF 18.00, a returns-based book test at CHF 16.90, a published consensus target near CHF 18.40) cluster in the same place. Against roughly CHF 12.00 of downside if the revenue margin slides to its floor and the cost ratio stays put, that is the wrong shape. The peer file's 'cheap versus peers' label does not survive live multiples: measured correctly, EFG trades roughly in line with Julius Baer and Vontobel on earnings while earning a higher return on capital -- a modest relative-value edge, not a discount.

On the regime: this thesis needs no rate cut, which counts in its favour when rate-rescue cases are being penalised, and its driver -- Swiss private-banking inflows and the fee margin -- is largely independent of both the artificial-intelligence capital-spending factor and the oil shock that dominate the book's other positions. That independence is real and valuable. But it is not independent of the equity market itself: fee income is charged on client assets, so a drawdown hits revenue and multiple together. With positioning full and volatility cheap, that is a reason to wait rather than a reason to move.

So: wait for the wash-out, and name it. The level is CHF 14.00 or below -- about ten times the 2027 consensus of CHF 1.385 a share and roughly 2.1 times tangible book -- where the same franchise offers something like 25% to fair value instead of 7%. The alternative trigger, which does not require a lower price, is confirmation at the full-year 2026 results in roughly February 2027 that the commission margin held at 46 basis points for a second consecutive half and that cost-to-income has moved below 70%. Either would convert this from a watch item into a position. Today it is a fairly-priced good bank whose one unanswered question -- why the advisory and management fee margin fell sequentially -- is precisely the question that decides the case.
sop_fair_value: CHF 17.25 per share (range CHF 16.90 to CHF 18.40)
sop_breakdown:
Base case about CHF 17.25 a share. There is no reportable segment breakdown for EFG, so the parts here are the four income streams, valued separately by how durable each one is -- which is the honest way to value a private bank whose reported profit mixes a recurring fee annuity with rate-driven and run-off income. Starting from the first half of 2026 annualised, costs allocated across the lines in proportion to revenue (a 72.3% cost-to-income ratio) and taxed at the 17.5% rate EFG actually paid in 2025, on roughly 301 million shares:
-- Recurring fee and commission engine: CHF 868 million of annualised revenue (CHF 434 million in the half, up 20% year on year, commission margin steady at 46 basis points), about CHF 198 million after tax, at 16 times -- a premium to the Swiss peer group because it is capital-light and compounding: CHF 10.55 a share.
-- Net interest income: CHF 270 million annualised (down 12% year on year), about CHF 62 million after tax, at 8 times because it is shrinking with rates: CHF 1.65 a share.
-- Treasury swaps, trading and other: CHF 510 million annualised, about CHF 117 million after tax, at 8 times -- volume-driven income that management has described as the other side of the same equation as the falling interest line: CHF 3.10 a share.
-- Life insurance: CHF 65 million annualised, about CHF 15 million after tax, at 2 times because management guided in July 2026 that it winds down to zero within about two years: CHF 0.10 a share.
-- Plus capital held above the 12% internal floor. Common equity tier 1 is 15.0%; management sized the equivalent buffer at CHF 260 million when the ratio was 14.4%, so roughly CHF 250 million after the Quilvest close: CHF 0.85 a share.
-- Less a residual reserve of about CHF 150 million against the remaining legacy legal cases, since the exceptional line has not been empty in any recent period: minus CHF 0.50 a share.
Subtotal on today's run-rate: about CHF 15.70 a share. Rolled forward twelve months for the full-year Quilvest contribution and the first phase of the 2027 platform migration (consensus 2027 net profit of CHF 424 million against a CHF 392 million current run-rate, about 8% higher): about CHF 17.00.
Two overlays that do NOT apply and are worth naming, because both would badly distort the number. First, the screener's 'net cash of CHF 2.56 billion' is not a special-situation add-back: for a deposit-taking bank those balances are client money placed at central banks, and adding them would invent roughly CHF 8.50 a share, more than half the company's market value. Second, the CHF 0.65 dividend for 2025 has already been paid (ex-dividend 26 March 2026, paid 30 March 2026), so it is not a pending distribution.
Cross-checks on the CHF 17.25 base: 13 times the consensus 2027 earnings of CHF 1.385 a share gives CHF 18.00; a returns-based book-value test (22.4% return on tangible equity, 4% growth, 10% cost of equity, implying about 3.1 times the roughly CHF 5.45 a share of tangible equity attributable to ordinary shareholders) gives about CHF 16.90; and the published analyst consensus target was cut to about CHF 18.40 after the results. The cluster is CHF 16.90 to CHF 18.40.
risk_reward: At CHF 16.10 the reward is thin against the risk. Upside runs to a base sum-of-the-parts value of about CHF 17.25 a share, with a favourable case at about CHF 21.00 that requires the 2027 platform migration to deliver the cost synergies. Downside runs to about CHF 12.00 in the adverse case -- the revenue margin sliding to the 85 basis point floor, life insurance at zero, treasury income normalising and the cost ratio stuck near 72% -- and to roughly CHF 11.00 if a further legacy legal charge lands on top. There is no structural floor beneath the shares: this is a going concern trading at roughly two and a half times tangible book, so book value is a reference point, not a backstop, and the CHF 15.62 52-week low is a chart level rather than a protection. The picture only turns genuinely favourable nearer CHF 14, where the same franchise would be available at about ten times next year's consensus earnings.
peer_comps_note:
The peer file's 'cheap versus peers' verdict does not survive live multiples, and it matters why. That verdict leans on the screener's 73% revenue growth, a 1.8% return on invested capital and a price-to-free-cash-flow near zero. All three are accounting artifacts of a deposit-taking bank: the revenue jump is a gross-up of interest income (operating income actually grew 11% in 2025 and 7% in the first half of 2026), return on invested capital is meaningless when the balance sheet is the product, and the negative free cash flow is deposit and lending flows, not cash burn.
Priced live on 27 July 2026: Julius Baer at CHF 70.34 trades on roughly 12.7 times trailing earnings and about 3.1 times tangible book; Vontobel at CHF 82.90 on roughly 12.2 times and about 2.25 times tangible book; UBS at CHF 42.87 is a universal bank and only loosely comparable. EFG at CHF 16.10 trades on about 16.8 times trailing earnings -- that trailing figure is depressed by the CHF 59 million legal provision taken in the second half of 2025 -- and on roughly 13 times this year's consensus and 11.6 times next year's. On tangible book it is about 2.4 times total tangible equity, closer to 3 times the portion attributable to ordinary shareholders once the perpetual capital notes are stripped out.
So EFG is not cheap against its Swiss peers on earnings; it is roughly in line, while earning a materially higher return on tangible equity (22.4% against roughly 15-16% for Julius Baer and Vontobel on the same live data). Adjusted for that return it sits at a modest discount to Julius Baer and a modest premium to Vontobel -- a real but small relative-value edge, not a deep discount. One caution on reading the gap as alpha: all three names move on the same drivers -- Swiss and dollar interest rates, the franc, and the level of world equity markets, which sets the fee base -- so most of any spread is shared-factor movement rather than something specific to EFG. The genuinely idiosyncratic fact on the tape is that EFG fell about 11.5% in the three sessions after its results while Julius Baer trades within 7% of its own 52-week high. That is a single-name de-rating, and it is the reason this name is worth watching at all.
interrogator_dossier:
# EFG International AG (EFGN, SIX Swiss Exchange) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared 27 July 2026 · price used: CHF 16.10 (SIX Swiss Exchange, quoted in Swiss francs; prior close CHF 15.98) · market value about CHF 4.84 billion**

Transcripts reviewed: full-year 2025 results (18 February 2026) and first-half 2026 results (22 July 2026). EFG reports twice a year, not quarterly, so the two calls below are the company's two most recent reporting events.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

EFG International is a Zurich-based private bank — it manages money for wealthy families across Switzerland, Europe, Asia and Latin America and earns most of its income as a fee on the assets it looks after. Across the two calls the story is unusually consistent, which is itself a finding: management has been telling the same story for three years and the numbers have followed it.

**February 2026 (full-year 2025):** the framing was "we finished the 2023-2025 cycle in record shape." Chief executive Giorgio Pradelli led with net new money of CHF 11.3 billion (6.8% growth, described as the highest since the global financial crisis), assets under management of CHF 185 billion, and record net profit of CHF 325 million. Three acquisitions in twelve months were introduced as a *new* strand — "10 years from the acquisition of BSI, and we are very pleased that we have started a new series of acquisitions." Chief financial officer Dimitris Politis added the cycle framing: revenue up 31% over three years versus 8% in the prior cycle, cost-to-income down from roughly 84% in 2019 to 69.8%, earnings per share from CHF 0.30 to above CHF 1.

**July 2026 (first-half 2026):** the story did not shift, it scaled. Assets under management crossed CHF 200 billion for the first time on the day the Quilvest acquisition closed (21 July 2026). Net profit of CHF 185 million was the best half in the company's history. Return on tangible equity — profit measured against the shareholders' capital excluding goodwill — reached 22.4%, already above the 20% target set for 2028.

**What was quietly added:** a defensive frame around the revenue margin. In February the margin was a success story ("98 basis points compared to 96 last year"). By July it is something to be *defended*: "the margin has dropped from 97 basis points to 91 basis points. We've been good at defending, and we're keeping the revenue margin above the 90 basis point level." A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point; the revenue margin is simply the fee-and-interest income EFG earns on every franc of client assets. That yield is falling.

**What was quietly dropped:** the life-insurance contribution, which used to be an earnings line worth talking about, is now being talked *out* of the story — "we do expect it to wind down to zero as we move along in the next couple of years" (July 2026).

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Before the table, a warning that matters more than anything in it: **the screener's standard metrics do not work on a bank, and several of them are badly misleading here.**

| Screener metric | What it says | What it actually is |
|---|---|---|
| Net cash CHF 2.56 billion ("a genuine add-back") | Cash CHF 7.09 billion exceeds debt CHF 4.53 billion | **Not usable.** Those balances are client deposits placed at central banks, funded by client liabilities. Treating it as surplus value would add roughly CHF 8.50 a share — more than half the market value — out of thin air. |
| Free cash flow −CHF 2.43 billion (trailing twelve months) | Massive cash burn | An artifact of deposit and lending flows moving through a bank's cash-flow statement. EFG is not burning cash; it generated over 2 percentage points of capital organically in the half. |
| Return on invested capital 1.8% | Value-destroying | Meaningless for a bank, where the balance sheet is the product. The right measure is return on tangible equity: **22.4%**. |
| Altman-Z score 0.4 | Distress | Not applicable to deposit-taking institutions. Common equity tier 1 capital — the regulator's core solvency measure — is **15.0%**, against a 12% internal floor. |
| Revenue +73.1% year on year | Explosive growth | A presentation artifact: gross interest income was grossed up in the 2025 figures. Operating income actually grew **11%** in 2025 and **7%** in the first half of 2026. |

Now the real claims:

| Management claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record net profit" (Feb 2026) | CHF 325.2 million reported, up from CHF 321.6 million in 2024 and CHF 303.2 million in 2023 | **Holds** — but the increase over 2024 was only about 1%; the "record" is a thin one. Excluding one-off items management put it at CHF 339 million. |
| "Best semester ever, CHF 185 million" (Jul 2026) | Confirmed; return on tangible equity 22.4%, up 3 percentage points | **Holds**, and this is the genuinely strong number. But it **missed the analyst consensus by about 2%** (Vontobel's assessment, 22 July 2026) on softer-than-expected revenue. |
| Net new money above the 4-6% target range | 6.8% in 2025; 6.2% annualised in the first half of 2026; fifteenth consecutive half of positive inflows | **Holds cleanly.** This is the single most credible claim in the file — it is hard to fake and it has been repeated fifteen times. |
| "We've been good at defending the margin" | Revenue margin 98 basis points (2025) → 91 (first half 2026); reported coverage of the results slides puts the year-earlier figure at 104 including life insurance. Net interest income −12% to CHF 135 million | **Partially holds.** The *fee* margin held at 46 basis points and commission income rose 20% to CHF 434 million. The decline is concentrated in the interest line. "Defending" is fair for fees, generous for the total. |
| "Consistent 15% bottom-line growth every year" | Profit up 5% year on year in the first half (excluding a prior-year one-off gain) | **Does not yet hold.** Five is not fifteen. The gap is meant to close as the acquisitions contribute and costs migrate onto EFG's platform in 2027 — that is a promise, not a delivery. |

| Capital strength | Common equity tier 1 14.4% (end-2025) → 15.0%; total capital 18.3%; organic capital generation 2.3% in the half | **Holds, with a caveat management volunteered:** roughly 50 basis points of that generation is a non-cash add-back of share-based pay (about CHF 80-90 million a year), and the risk-weighted-asset optimisation that helped is largely finished — "the biggest part of it has already been concluded in the first half of 2026." **Where the story is richer than the numbers:** the phrase "record" is doing heavy lifting on a profit line that grew about 1% in 2025 and 5% in the first half of 2026. **Where the story is poorer than it needs to be:** management does not press its strongest point — that fee income grew 20% while the fee margin held — nearly hard enough, and instead lets the falling *total* revenue yield dominate the discussion.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising, but with a defensive undertow that was not there a year ago.**

February 2026 was straightforwardly offensive in tone: "the operating business is firing on all cylinders," "we have started a new series of acquisitions," "record" used five times in the opening remarks. Pradelli was expansive about capital deployment.

July 2026 is more confident on outcomes and more careful on drivers. Pradelli opens with genuine pride — "for the first time ever, EFG was able to cross the CHF 200 billion mark" — and volunteers the humility line, "I don't want to enter into debate whether size matters or not." Politis's confidence is concrete and numerate: "the actual bottom line of the first half of this year of CHF 185 million is practically the bottom line we had for the full year back in 2022."

But the vocabulary around revenue has turned protective. Compare February's "defending or expanding the margin has been very successful" with July's "in an environment of dropping interest rates, that was the only set of actions that could actually increase our profitability." The second sentence concedes that the tailwind is gone. Politis then adds a conditional that did not appear in February: "margins can be higher, margins can be lower, and we need to compensate."

Specificity of guidance has, notably, **increased** rather than decreased — a good sign. Politis gives an exact target architecture (four numbers for 2028), an exact commitment ("approximately 15% growth in bottom line every single year in this strategic cycle"), and quantifies the non-cash capital add-back unprompted when challenged.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium-High.**

The evidence splits cleanly in two directions.

**They deliver on their own multi-year targets.** The 2023-2025 cycle was closed on plan: revenue up 31%, cost-to-income from above 84% to below 70%, earnings per share from CHF 0.30 to above CHF 1.00, five consecutive dividend increases (the CHF 0.65 for 2025 was approved at the 20 March 2026 annual meeting and paid 30 March 2026 — it is already in shareholders' hands, not a pending distribution). Three of the four 2026-2028 targets were already met in the *first* semester of the cycle: return on tangible equity 22.4% against a 20% goal, net new money 6.2% against 4-6%, revenue margin 91 basis points against a floor of 85. That is a management team that sets targets it can hit.

**They miss the analysts' near-term numbers.** The screener records zero beats in four reporting periods — and while that metric is partly an artifact (EFG reports semi-annually, so a "quarterly" beat rate is not well defined), the most recent print is unambiguous: the first-half 2026 profit came in about 2% below consensus on weaker revenue, and the shares fell.

There is also a small piece of **sandbagging discipline worth crediting**: management pre-committed in November 2025 to a revenue margin "in excess of 85" basis points and told the market the landing point would be "somewhere in the middle" between 95 and 85. It landed at 90-91. They called their own number correctly nine months out. That is unusual and it counts.

The honest summary: trust the three-year architecture, discount the six-month precision.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three recurring pressure points, one of which produced a genuine non-answer.

**The fee margin decomposition — the real one.** In July 2026 Nicholas Herman put the sharpest question of either call: management's slide shows the recurring commission margin stable, but "if I look at the advisory and management fees … as a percentage of your average [assets under management], so effectively calculates an advisory and management fee margin, that is down sequentially." Politis did not answer it. He replied that "you cannot just strip out one line and do the calculation. You need to go into breakdowns of all the lines" — a methodological objection, not a number. Herman pushed a second time on whether performance fees had flattered the prior half; Politis said "nothing very material." Pradelli then partly conceded the point on management's behalf: "if you look, especially in this half, the volume effect was more important than the margin effect." Translated: assets grew, the price per franc of assets did not. **This is the single most important unanswered question in the file**, because the fee margin is the moat.

**The legacy litigation tail.** Hannah Leivdal of Citi asked in February 2026 what gives management confidence that no further provisions are coming against the outstanding legal cases in the annual report. Politis's answer was capital-based, not case-based: 14.4% common equity tier 1, CHF 260 million of excess capital over the internal 12% floor, and the claim that the recent CHF 59 million provision "derisked the largest single risk item we had." He did not say the remaining cases are small. Note the shape of the recent record: a CHF 45 million insurance recovery in the first half of 2025, a CHF 59 million provision in the second half — the exceptional line is never empty.

**The treasury swap line — where management answered honestly and revealed something.** Asked twice, in February and again in July, why swap income rose while the rate differential narrowed, Politis gave the same answer both times: volume, not margin. Then in February he added the sentence that matters: "what also happened is that the NII element decreased because it's the other side of the same equation." Management is telling you that part of the reported income growth is an accounting relocation of net interest income, not new economics. Nobody on either call followed up on that.

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing:** mandate penetration — the share of client assets under a paid advisory or discretionary mandate — has been **stuck at 67% against a 75% goal**, and Pradelli's answer was a list of intentions ("we are going to put in place all a set of actions") with an explicit disclaimer, "there is no guarantee on the outcomes."

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The revenue yield is falling faster than management's framing suggests.** Ninety-one basis points in the first half of 2026 against 97 a year earlier on management's own comparison, and 104 on the reported basis that includes life insurance. Net interest income fell 12% to CHF 135 million.

🔴 **Cost-to-income moved the wrong way** — 69.8% for 2025 to 71.5% in the first half of 2026, leaving the one missed target 350 basis points away with two and a half years to run.

🔴 **Earnings quality is mixed.** Two of the income streams are explicitly non-durable: life insurance is guided to zero within about two years (July 2026), and treasury swap income is management-acknowledged as the mirror image of the shrinking interest line (February 2026).

🔴 **The exceptional line is a permanent fixture.** A recovery one half, a provision the next. Trailing-twelve-month profitability carries roughly CHF 107 million of one-off loss (Simply Wall St, 23 July 2026) — which is why the trailing net margin reads 16.3% against 23.3% a year earlier.

🔴 **Capital generation is partly non-repeatable**, on management's own account: about 50 basis points of the 2.3% organic build is a non-cash share-based-pay add-back, and the risk-weighted-asset optimisation is largely done.

🔴 **The share register is closed.** EFG Bank European Financial Group — the Latsis family vehicle — holds roughly 45%, and BTG Pactual retains roughly 13-17% (down from the 30% it took when it sold BSI to EFG in 2016). With about 60% locked up and daily volume around 250,000 shares, any further BTG sell-down is a mechanical overhang on a thin float, and there is no realistic path for a takeover premium or an activist.

🟢 **Fifteen consecutive halves of positive net new money**, running at 6.2% annualised against a 4-6% target. This is the hardest number in the file to fake and the strongest evidence of a real franchise.

🟢 **Fee income is growing three times faster than total revenue** — net commission income up 20% to CHF 434 million in the first half of 2026, with the commission margin steady at 46 basis points. The part of the business that constitutes the moat is compounding.

🟢 **Return on tangible equity rose 3 percentage points to 22.4%**, clearing the 2028 target in the first semester of the cycle. Rising returns on capital are the opposite of an eroding franchise.

🟢 **Capital is genuinely strong**: common equity tier 1 15.0%, total capital 18.3%, liquidity coverage 270% at end-2025, and a fifth consecutive dividend increase.

🟢 **Management called its own margin landing point correctly** nine months ahead ("somewhere in the middle" between 95 and 85 basis points; landed at 90-91).

🟢 **Talent flow is running in EFG's direction** — 79 client relationship officers signed in 2025, with Pradelli noting in July 2026 that "some of the big banks have changed their strategy" and EFG is hiring on the back of it.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Right tech, not fintech."** Asked about the Lia artificial-intelligence platform in February 2026, Pradelli was refreshingly unhyped: the use cases are compliance, risk and back-office efficiency, and client experience is "the next level, but we are not there yet." A management team that declines to oversell an AI story is usually telling you the truth elsewhere too.

**The word "quality" doing new work.** In July 2026 Pradelli pre-empts the scale question — "at EFG we are very much focused on quality, not only quantity" — before anyone asks it. Politis echoes it: "not just about the actual quantity of our profit, but also the quality of our profit." When two executives independently reach for the same defensive framing in one call, the market has been asking whether the growth is bought rather than earned. It partly is: assets rose 23% year on year, but organic net new money was 6.2%.

**Acquisition contribution is being deferred, not delivered.** In February 2026 the two closed deals were a "small single-digit negative" on profit. In July 2026 they are "already contributing profits" but the real benefit is pushed out: "we do expect a higher contribution, especially after the technology migration" — that is 2027. The cost synergies underwriting the 68% cost-to-income target all sit beyond the next reporting event.

**Geography is being described in aggregate, deliberately.** Asked to name the strongest markets in July 2026, Pradelli named Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia and New Zealand, then closed the door: "I wouldn't highlight any specific country or location." Compare that with the precision he brings to net new money and capital. Aggregation is where management is least comfortable being held to account.

**Currency risk is acknowledged and then minimised.** The US dollar is 47% of client assets and was flagged as a 2025 headwind that "most probably will remain [a headwind] in 2026." Asked in February 2026 whether clients were rotating out of the dollar, Politis said the mix is unchanged at 47% and dismissed the anecdotes. He is probably right — but a bank whose fee base is nearly half dollar-denominated, reporting in Swiss francs, has a translation exposure it does not hedge away.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.**

This is a real franchise getting better at what it does. Fifteen consecutive halves of positive client inflows, a return on tangible equity that rose three percentage points to 22.4% and cleared the 2028 target at the start of the cycle, fee income growing 20% with a stable fee margin, capital at 15.0%, and a management team that has hit the multi-year targets it set for itself. Nothing in either transcript looks evasive on the numbers that matter most.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *the quality of the earnings, not their level.* Record profit of CHF 185 million rests on four income streams of very different durability — a growing fee engine (durable), a shrinking interest line (cyclical), treasury swap income that management has admitted is the accounting mirror of that shrinking interest line, and a life-insurance contribution being guided to zero. Underwrite the fee engine at a full multiple and everything else at a discount, and the intrinsic value lands close to where the shares already trade. The shares are not expensive; they are also not the deep discount the raw screen implies, because the raw screen is measuring a bank with tools built for an industrial company.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat type is *switching costs plus intangible relationship capital* — wealthy families do not move custodians casually, and the client relationship officer who holds the relationship is the true asset. That is a real moat, and the fifteen-half inflow record proves it. But it is narrow for three reasons: the asset walks (EFG itself hired 79 relationship officers away from competitors in 2025, which cuts both ways); at CHF 200 billion EFG is subscale against UBS's global wealth business; and the price it can charge per franc of assets is visibly under pressure. Regulatory-licence value in Swiss private banking is real but shared with every competitor.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Resist the temptation to read the falling revenue margin as erosion. The *fee* margin — the part that is actually the moat — held at 46 basis points while fee income rose 20%, and return on tangible equity is rising, not falling. The decline sits in the rate-driven interest line, which is a cycle, not a franchise. The number that would change this verdict is the commission margin itself: if 46 basis points starts sliding, the moat is eroding and the whole case changes. That is precisely the question Nicholas Herman asked in July 2026 and did not get answered.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** Private banking for the wealthy is among the businesses least exposed to the structural forces currently hollowing out incumbents. Generative artificial intelligence compresses the cost of advice but does not replace the trust, tax and jurisdictional complexity that a family with CHF 50 million actually pays for — and EFG is deploying it on its own cost base rather than being disrupted by it. Passive investing and fee transparency exert steady, gradual pressure on the price of advice, which is a headwind to the margin but not a threat to the terminal value.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a shrinking base?** Neither, quite. The shares fell about 11.5% over three sessions after the 22 July results — from CHF 18.08 on 21 July to CHF 15.98 on 24 July — on a 2% profit miss, while Julius Baer trades within 7% of its own 52-week high. That is a single-name de-rating, not a sector event, and it is an over-reaction to the headline. But the base is not shrinking and the starting valuation was not distressed, so the correction mostly removed an optimism premium rather than creating a discount. What is left is a good business at a fair price, with the interesting entry a further leg lower away.

bull_thesis:
EFG International is a Zurich-based private bank -- it looks after the money of wealthy families across Switzerland, Europe, Asia and Latin America and is paid a fee on the assets it holds. The bull case is that this is a genuinely good franchise that just got marked down for the wrong reason.

Start with what is hard to fake. Client money has flowed in for fifteen consecutive half-years. In the first half of 2026 net new assets were CHF 5.7 billion, an annualised 6.2%, above the company's own 4-6% target range, and that follows CHF 11.3 billion (6.8%) in 2025. Assets under management crossed CHF 200 billion for the first time on 21 July 2026 when the Quilvest acquisition closed, up 23% in a year. Net profit for the half was CHF 185 million, the best six months in the company's history, and return on tangible equity -- profit measured against shareholders' capital excluding goodwill -- reached 22.4%, up three percentage points and already above the 20% goal set for 2028. Three of the four targets for the 2026-2028 cycle were met in the very first semester of that cycle.

Then look at where the growth is coming from. Net commission income, the recurring fee stream that is the actual moat, rose 20% to CHF 434 million while the commission margin held steady at 46 basis points (a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point). The part of the revenue that fell is the interest line -- down 12% to CHF 135 million as rates came down. That is a cycle, not a franchise problem, and it is exactly the distinction the market failed to make on 22 and 23 July, when the shares fell about 11.5% over three sessions on a profit that missed consensus by roughly 2%.

The balance sheet supports the case rather than threatening it. Common equity tier 1 capital -- the regulator's core solvency measure -- rose 100 basis points to 15.0% against a 12% internal floor, total capital is 18.3%, and the company generated 2.3% of capital organically in the half. The dividend has risen five years running; the CHF 0.65 for 2025 was paid on 30 March 2026. Management has also earned some benefit of the doubt: in November 2025 it told the market the revenue margin would land 'somewhere in the middle' between 95 and 85 basis points, and it landed at 90-91.

Finally, the profit engine has room to improve that is already contracted for. The cost-to-income ratio is 71.5% against a 68% target, and the gap exists because the acquired banks -- Cite Gestion, the New Zealand business and now Quilvest -- have not yet been migrated onto EFG's technology platform. That migration is scheduled for 2027. If it lands, the same revenue produces materially more profit, which is how management gets from the 5% growth it delivered this half to the roughly 15% a year it has promised for the cycle.

Conditions this case depends on: the commission margin holds at or near 46 basis points; net new money stays inside or above the 4-6% range; the 2027 platform migration delivers the cost synergies on schedule; world equity markets do not fall materially, since fee income moves with the value of client assets; and no new legacy legal provision of consequence lands.

Mandate penetration, the share of client assets under a paid advisory or discretionary mandate, has been stuck at 67% against a 75% goal, and the plan to fix it came with the disclaimer 'there is no guarantee on the outcomes.'

Cost-to-income was 69.8% for 2025 and 71.5% in the first half of 2026, leaving the one missed target 350 basis points away, with the fix -- the 2027 technology migration -- entirely in the future. Every cost synergy underwriting the 68% goal sits beyond the next reporting event, which is not until roughly February 2027.

A CHF 45 million insurance recovery in the first half of 2025, a CHF 59 million provision in the second half; the trailing twelve months carry roughly CHF 107 million of one-off loss, which is why the trailing net margin reads 16.3% against 23.3% a year earlier. # EFG International AG (EFGN, SIX Swiss Exchange) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared 27 July 2026 · price used: CHF 16.10 (SIX Swiss Exchange, quoted in Swiss francs; prior close CHF 15.98) · market value about CHF 4.84 billion**

Transcripts reviewed: full-year 2025 results (18 February 2026) and first-half 2026 results (22 July 2026). EFG reports twice a year, not quarterly, so the two calls below are the company's two most recent reporting events.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

EFG International is a Zurich-based private bank — it manages money for wealthy families across Switzerland, Europe, Asia and Latin America and earns most of its income as a fee on the assets it looks after. Across the two calls the story is unusually consistent, which is itself a finding: management has been telling the same story for three years and the numbers have followed it.

**February 2026 (full-year 2025):** the framing was "we finished the 2023-2025 cycle in record shape." Chief executive Giorgio Pradelli led with net new money of CHF 11.3 billion (6.8% growth, described as the highest since the global financial crisis), assets under management of CHF 185 billion, and record net profit of CHF 325 million. Three acquisitions in twelve months were introduced as a *new* strand — "10 years from the acquisition of BSI, and we are very pleased that we have started a new series of acquisitions." Chief financial officer Dimitris Politis added the cycle framing: revenue up 31% over three years versus 8% in the prior cycle, cost-to-income down from roughly 84% in 2019 to 69.8%, earnings per share from CHF 0.30 to above CHF 1.

**July 2026 (first-half 2026):** the story did not shift, it scaled. Assets under management crossed CHF 200 billion for the first time on the day the Quilvest acquisition closed (21 July 2026). Net profit of CHF 185 million was the best half in the company's history. Return on tangible equity — profit measured against the shareholders' capital excluding goodwill — reached 22.4%, already above the 20% target set for 2028.

**What was quietly added:** a defensive frame around the revenue margin. In February the margin was a success story ("98 basis points compared to 96 last year"). By July it is something to be *defended*: "the margin has dropped from 97 basis points to 91 basis points. We've been good at defending, and we're keeping the revenue margin above the 90 basis point level." A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point; the revenue margin is simply the fee-and-interest income EFG earns on every franc of client assets. That yield is falling.

**What was quietly dropped:** the life-insurance contribution, which used to be an earnings line worth talking about, is now being talked *out* of the story — "we do expect it to wind down to zero as we move along in the next couple of years" (July 2026).

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Before the table, a warning that matters more than anything in it: **the screener's standard metrics do not work on a bank, and several of them are badly misleading here.**

| Screener metric | What it says | What it actually is |
|---|---|---|
| Net cash CHF 2.56 billion ("a genuine add-back") | Cash CHF 7.09 billion exceeds debt CHF 4.53 billion | **Not usable.** Those balances are client deposits placed at central banks, funded by client liabilities. Treating it as surplus value would add roughly CHF 8.50 a share — more than half the market value — out of thin air. |
| Free cash flow −CHF 2.43 billion (trailing twelve months) | Massive cash burn | An artifact of deposit and lending flows moving through a bank's cash-flow statement. EFG is not burning cash; it generated over 2 percentage points of capital organically in the half. |
| Return on invested capital 1.8% | Value-destroying | Meaningless for a bank, where the balance sheet is the product. The right measure is return on tangible equity: **22.4%**. |
| Altman-Z score 0.4 | Distress | Not applicable to deposit-taking institutions. Common equity tier 1 capital — the regulator's core solvency measure — is **15.0%**, against a 12% internal floor. |
| Revenue +73.1% year on year | Explosive growth | A presentation artifact: gross interest income was grossed up in the 2025 figures. Operating income actually grew **11%** in 2025 and **7%** in the first half of 2026. |

Now the real claims:

| Management claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record net profit" (Feb 2026) | CHF 325.2 million reported, up from CHF 321.6 million in 2024 and CHF 303.2 million in 2023 | **Holds** — but the increase over 2024 was only about 1%; the "record" is a thin one. Excluding one-off items management put it at CHF 339 million. |
| "Best semester ever, CHF 185 million" (Jul 2026) | Confirmed; return on tangible equity 22.4%, up 3 percentage points | **Holds**, and this is the genuinely strong number. But it **missed the analyst consensus by about 2%** (Vontobel's assessment, 22 July 2026) on softer-than-expected revenue. |
| Net new money above the 4-6% target range | 6.8% in 2025; 6.2% annualised in the first half of 2026; fifteenth consecutive half of positive inflows | **Holds cleanly.** This is the single most credible claim in the file — it is hard to fake and it has been repeated fifteen times. |
| "We've been good at defending the margin" | Revenue margin 98 basis points (2025) → 91 (first half 2026); reported coverage of the results slides puts the year-earlier figure at 104 including life insurance. Net interest income −12% to CHF 135 million | **Partially holds.** The *fee* margin held at 46 basis points and commission income rose 20% to CHF 434 million. The decline is concentrated in the interest line. "Defending" is fair for fees, generous for the total. |
| "Consistent 15% bottom-line growth every year" | Profit up 5% year on year in the first half (excluding a prior-year one-off gain) | **Does not yet hold.** Five is not fifteen. The gap is meant to close as the acquisitions contribute and costs migrate onto EFG's platform in 2027 — that is a promise, not a delivery. |
| Cost discipline | Cost-to-income 69.8% (2025) → **71.5%** (first half 2026), against a 68% target for 2028 | **Went backwards.** Management attributes this to acquisition costs. It is the one target of four that is being missed, by 350 basis points. |
| Capital strength | Common equity tier 1 14.4% (end-2025) → 15.0%; total capital 18.3%; organic capital generation 2.3% in the half | **Holds, with a caveat management volunteered:** roughly 50 basis points of that generation is a non-cash add-back of share-based pay (about CHF 80-90 million a year), and the risk-weighted-asset optimisation that helped is largely finished — "the biggest part of it has already been concluded in the first half of 2026." The capital build is therefore less repeatable than it looks. |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers:** the phrase "record" is doing heavy lifting on a profit line that grew about 1% in 2025 and 5% in the first half of 2026. **Where the story is poorer than it needs to be:** management does not press its strongest point — that fee income grew 20% while the fee margin held — nearly hard enough, and instead lets the falling *total* revenue yield dominate the discussion.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising, but with a defensive undertow that was not there a year ago.**

February 2026 was straightforwardly offensive in tone: "the operating business is firing on all cylinders," "we have started a new series of acquisitions," "record" used five times in the opening remarks. Pradelli was expansive about capital deployment.

July 2026 is more confident on outcomes and more careful on drivers. Pradelli opens with genuine pride — "for the first time ever, EFG was able to cross the CHF 200 billion mark" — and volunteers the humility line, "I don't want to enter into debate whether size matters or not." Politis's confidence is concrete and numerate: "the actual bottom line of the first half of this year of CHF 185 million is practically the bottom line we had for the full year back in 2022."

But the vocabulary around revenue has turned protective. Compare February's "defending or expanding the margin has been very successful" with July's "in an environment of dropping interest rates, that was the only set of actions that could actually increase our profitability." The second sentence concedes that the tailwind is gone. Politis then adds a conditional that did not appear in February: "margins can be higher, margins can be lower, and we need to compensate."

Specificity of guidance has, notably, **increased** rather than decreased — a good sign. Politis gives an exact target architecture (four numbers for 2028), an exact commitment ("approximately 15% growth in bottom line every single year in this strategic cycle"), and quantifies the non-cash capital add-back unprompted when challenged.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium-High.**

The evidence splits cleanly in two directions.

**They deliver on their own multi-year targets.** The 2023-2025 cycle was closed on plan: revenue up 31%, cost-to-income from above 84% to below 70%, earnings per share from CHF 0.30 to above CHF 1.00, five consecutive dividend increases (the CHF 0.65 for 2025 was approved at the 20 March 2026 annual meeting and paid 30 March 2026 — it is already in shareholders' hands, not a pending distribution). Three of the four 2026-2028 targets were already met in the *first* semester of the cycle: return on tangible equity 22.4% against a 20% goal, net new money 6.2% against 4-6%, revenue margin 91 basis points against a floor of 85. That is a management team that sets targets it can hit.

**They miss the analysts' near-term numbers.** The screener records zero beats in four reporting periods — and while that metric is partly an artifact (EFG reports semi-annually, so a "quarterly" beat rate is not well defined), the most recent print is unambiguous: the first-half 2026 profit came in about 2% below consensus on weaker revenue, and the shares fell.

There is also a small piece of **sandbagging discipline worth crediting**: management pre-committed in November 2025 to a revenue margin "in excess of 85" basis points and told the market the landing point would be "somewhere in the middle" between 95 and 85. It landed at 90-91. They called their own number correctly nine months out. That is unusual and it counts.

The honest summary: trust the three-year architecture, discount the six-month precision.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three recurring pressure points, one of which produced a genuine non-answer.

**The fee margin decomposition — the real one.** In July 2026 Nicholas Herman put the sharpest question of either call: management's slide shows the recurring commission margin stable, but "if I look at the advisory and management fees … as a percentage of your average [assets under management], so effectively calculates an advisory and management fee margin, that is down sequentially." Politis did not answer it. He replied that "you cannot just strip out one line and do the calculation. You need to go into breakdowns of all the lines" — a methodological objection, not a number. Herman pushed a second time on whether performance fees had flattered the prior half; Politis said "nothing very material." Pradelli then partly conceded the point on management's behalf: "if you look, especially in this half, the volume effect was more important than the margin effect." Translated: assets grew, the price per franc of assets did not. **This is the single most important unanswered question in the file**, because the fee margin is the moat.

**The legacy litigation tail.** Hannah Leivdal of Citi asked in February 2026 what gives management confidence that no further provisions are coming against the outstanding legal cases in the annual report. Politis's answer was capital-based, not case-based: 14.4% common equity tier 1, CHF 260 million of excess capital over the internal 12% floor, and the claim that the recent CHF 59 million provision "derisked the largest single risk item we had." He did not say the remaining cases are small. Note the shape of the recent record: a CHF 45 million insurance recovery in the first half of 2025, a CHF 59 million provision in the second half — the exceptional line is never empty.

**The treasury swap line — where management answered honestly and revealed something.** Asked twice, in February and again in July, why swap income rose while the rate differential narrowed, Politis gave the same answer both times: volume, not margin. Then in February he added the sentence that matters: "what also happened is that the NII element decreased because it's the other side of the same equation." Management is telling you that part of the reported income growth is an accounting relocation of net interest income, not new economics. Nobody on either call followed up on that.

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing:** mandate penetration — the share of client assets under a paid advisory or discretionary mandate — has been **stuck at 67% against a 75% goal**, and Pradelli's answer was a list of intentions ("we are going to put in place all a set of actions") with an explicit disclaimer, "there is no guarantee on the outcomes."

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The revenue yield is falling faster than management's framing suggests.** Ninety-one basis points in the first half of 2026 against 97 a year earlier on management's own comparison, and 104 on the reported basis that includes life insurance. Net interest income fell 12% to CHF 135 million.

🔴 **Cost-to-income moved the wrong way** — 69.8% for 2025 to 71.5% in the first half of 2026, leaving the one missed target 350 basis points away with two and a half years to run.

🔴 **Earnings quality is mixed.** Two of the income streams are explicitly non-durable: life insurance is guided to zero within about two years (July 2026), and treasury swap income is management-acknowledged as the mirror image of the shrinking interest line (February 2026).

🔴 **The exceptional line is a permanent fixture.** A recovery one half, a provision the next. Trailing-twelve-month profitability carries roughly CHF 107 million of one-off loss (Simply Wall St, 23 July 2026) — which is why the trailing net margin reads 16.3% against 23.3% a year earlier.

🔴 **Capital generation is partly non-repeatable**, on management's own account: about 50 basis points of the 2.3% organic build is a non-cash share-based-pay add-back, and the risk-weighted-asset optimisation is largely done.

🔴 **The share register is closed.** EFG Bank European Financial Group — the Latsis family vehicle — holds roughly 45%, and BTG Pactual retains roughly 13-17% (down from the 30% it took when it sold BSI to EFG in 2016). With about 60% locked up and daily volume around 250,000 shares, any further BTG sell-down is a mechanical overhang on a thin float, and there is no realistic path for a takeover premium or an activist.

🟢 **Fifteen consecutive halves of positive net new money**, running at 6.2% annualised against a 4-6% target. This is the hardest number in the file to fake and the strongest evidence of a real franchise.

🟢 **Fee income is growing three times faster than total revenue** — net commission income up 20% to CHF 434 million in the first half of 2026, with the commission margin steady at 46 basis points. The part of the business that constitutes the moat is compounding.

🟢 **Return on tangible equity rose 3 percentage points to 22.4%**, clearing the 2028 target in the first semester of the cycle. Rising returns on capital are the opposite of an eroding franchise.

🟢 **Capital is genuinely strong**: common equity tier 1 15.0%, total capital 18.3%, liquidity coverage 270% at end-2025, and a fifth consecutive dividend increase.

🟢 **Management called its own margin landing point correctly** nine months ahead ("somewhere in the middle" between 95 and 85 basis points; landed at 90-91).

🟢 **Talent flow is running in EFG's direction** — 79 client relationship officers signed in 2025, with Pradelli noting in July 2026 that "some of the big banks have changed their strategy" and EFG is hiring on the back of it.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Right tech, not fintech."** Asked about the Lia artificial-intelligence platform in February 2026, Pradelli was refreshingly unhyped: the use cases are compliance, risk and back-office efficiency, and client experience is "the next level, but we are not there yet." A management team that declines to oversell an AI story is usually telling you the truth elsewhere too.

**The word "quality" doing new work.** In July 2026 Pradelli pre-empts the scale question — "at EFG we are very much focused on quality, not only quantity" — before anyone asks it. Politis echoes it: "not just about the actual quantity of our profit, but also the quality of our profit." When two executives independently reach for the same defensive framing in one call, the market has been asking whether the growth is bought rather than earned. It partly is: assets rose 23% year on year, but organic net new money was 6.2%.

**Acquisition contribution is being deferred, not delivered.** In February 2026 the two closed deals were a "small single-digit negative" on profit. In July 2026 they are "already contributing profits" but the real benefit is pushed out: "we do expect a higher contribution, especially after the technology migration" — that is 2027. The cost synergies underwriting the 68% cost-to-income target all sit beyond the next reporting event.

**Geography is being described in aggregate, deliberately.** Asked to name the strongest markets in July 2026, Pradelli named Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia and New Zealand, then closed the door: "I wouldn't highlight any specific country or location." Compare that with the precision he brings to net new money and capital. Aggregation is where management is least comfortable being held to account.

**Currency risk is acknowledged and then minimised.** The US dollar is 47% of client assets and was flagged as a 2025 headwind that "most probably will remain [a headwind] in 2026." Asked in February 2026 whether clients were rotating out of the dollar, Politis said the mix is unchanged at 47% and dismissed the anecdotes. He is probably right — but a bank whose fee base is nearly half dollar-denominated, reporting in Swiss francs, has a translation exposure it does not hedge away.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.**

This is a real franchise getting better at what it does. Fifteen consecutive halves of positive client inflows, a return on tangible equity that rose three percentage points to 22.4% and cleared the 2028 target at the start of the cycle, fee income growing 20% with a stable fee margin, capital at 15.0%, and a management team that has hit the multi-year targets it set for itself. Nothing in either transcript looks evasive on the numbers that matter most.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *the quality of the earnings, not their level.* Record profit of CHF 185 million rests on four income streams of very different durability — a growing fee engine (durable), a shrinking interest line (cyclical), treasury swap income that management has admitted is the accounting mirror of that shrinking interest line, and a life-insurance contribution being guided to zero. Underwrite the fee engine at a full multiple and everything else at a discount, and the intrinsic value lands close to where the shares already trade. The shares are not expensive; they are also not the deep discount the raw screen implies, because the raw screen is measuring a bank with tools built for an industrial company.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat type is *switching costs plus intangible relationship capital* — wealthy families do not move custodians casually, and the client relationship officer who holds the relationship is the true asset. That is a real moat, and the fifteen-half inflow record proves it. But it is narrow for three reasons: the asset walks (EFG itself hired 79 relationship officers away from competitors in 2025, which cuts both ways); at CHF 200 billion EFG is subscale against UBS's global wealth business; and the price it can charge per franc of assets is visibly under pressure. Regulatory-licence value in Swiss private banking is real but shared with every competitor.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Resist the temptation to read the falling revenue margin as erosion. The *fee* margin — the part that is actually the moat — held at 46 basis points while fee income rose 20%, and return on tangible equity is rising, not falling. The decline sits in the rate-driven interest line, which is a cycle, not a franchise. The number that would change this verdict is the commission margin itself: if 46 basis points starts sliding, the moat is eroding and the whole case changes. That is precisely the question Nicholas Herman asked in July 2026 and did not get answered.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** Private banking for the wealthy is among the businesses least exposed to the structural forces currently hollowing out incumbents. Generative artificial intelligence compresses the cost of advice but does not replace the trust, tax and jurisdictional complexity that a family with CHF 50 million actually pays for — and EFG is deploying it on its own cost base rather than being disrupted by it. Passive investing and fee transparency exert steady, gradual pressure on the price of advice, which is a headwind to the margin but not a threat to the terminal value.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a shrinking base?** Neither, quite. The shares fell about 11.5% over three sessions after the 22 July results — from CHF 18.08 on 21 July to CHF 15.98 on 24 July — on a 2% profit miss, while Julius Baer trades within 7% of its own 52-week high. That is a single-name de-rating, not a sector event, and it is an over-reaction to the headline. But the base is not shrinking and the starting valuation was not distressed, so the correction mostly removed an optimism premium rather than creating a discount. What is left is a good business at a fair price, with the interesting entry a further leg lower away.

---
